title: Next year in Jerusalem
hookLine: long before any movement, Jewish prayer faced Jerusalem

lines: THE LAST LINE OF THE SEDER.
cards: It's late on the first night of Passover. The matzah is crumbs, the glasses refilled again and again, and a child is asleep across two chairs.
Then, at the very end of the Haggadah, the table says one line together, sometimes sung, sometimes shouted: next year in Jerusalem.

The same words come back at the close of Yom Kippur, after a whole day of fasting, as the last long blast of the shofar fades. Two great nights of the Jewish year end in the same place. Not in the room.

teach.b: The line rests on something Jews do every day: they pray facing Jerusalem. The roots are in the Tanakh.
When Solomon dedicates the Temple, in the First Book of Kings, he asks God to hear people even when they are far away, if they pray toward the land, the city and the house.
In the Book of Daniel, Daniel in Babylon goes up to his room, where the windows open toward Jerusalem, and prays there.
The Talmud turns this into circles, one inside the next. Someone praying outside the land of Israel turns toward the land. Someone in the land turns toward Jerusalem.
Someone in Jerusalem turns toward the Temple. Someone in the Temple turns toward its innermost room. So a whole scattered people, from every direction, leans in toward one point.

teach.h: IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM.
teach.b: The psalm of the exiles puts it as a vow: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." So what does next year in Jerusalem mean? Jews hear it in more than one way.
For some, it is a plain hope to stand in the city. For some, it waits for the days of the Messiah and a rebuilt Temple. For some, it is a picture of a world repaired.
And at seders in Jerusalem itself, some people add a word: next year in Jerusalem rebuilt. Even there, the line points somewhere further. This longing came long before any political plan.
In the days ahead, people answer it in very different ways.

how: Jews traditionally face toward Jerusalem when they say the Amidah, the standing prayer, and the words next year in Jerusalem close the Passover seder and the final service of Yom Kippur.

o: another name for the whole land of Israel
the city Jews turn to face when they pray
the Temple's innermost and holiest room

games.q: next year in jerusalem — tap the pairs.
p: asks God to hear prayers toward the city
circles of direction, one inside the next
ends with next year in Jerusalem

s: next year in Jerusalem is said only at Passover
it also closes Yom Kippur, after the last blast of the shofar.
in the Talmud, someone praying in Jerusalem turns toward the Temple
outside the land, toward the land; in the land, toward Jerusalem; in Jerusalem, toward the Temple.
the line has one meaning that every Jew shares
some hear a hope to visit, some the days of the Messiah, some a world repaired.

games.q: you are Daniel, far from home in Babylon. it's time to pray. where do you go?
o: to a room whose windows open toward Jerusalem.
games.why: the Book of Daniel says he went up to his room, with windows open toward Jerusalem, and prayed there.

practice: If you know which way Jerusalem lies from where you are, turn your chair or your body that way; if not, take your best guess, since the Talmud's circles are about leaning in, not about a compass.
If you pray, say the psalm's line quietly, if I forget thee, O Jerusalem; if you don't, just hold the idea of one place a people has kept facing.

wordCard.voice: Jerusalem. The city Jews turn to face in prayer from everywhere in the world, the place the seder and Yom Kippur both close toward. Today's word.

orig.note: next year in Jerusalem, as it is said at the end of the seder.

carryVoice: Your line: leaning toward one point. The longing is old, and the answers are about to multiply. See you tomorrow.
